title: Nervous system: brain, cord and nerves
note: neur/o means nerve; encephal/o is the whole brain, cerebr/o the cerebrum and cerebell/o the cerebellum; mening/o names the protective membranes. Function suffixes: -plegia paralysis, -paresis slight paralysis or weakness, -phasia speech, -esthesia sensation, -algesia sensitivity to pain.

read.title: Coverings, parts and functions
text: The nervous system has two divisions. The central nervous system is the brain (encephal/o) and spinal cord (myel/o). The peripheral nervous system is every nerve (neur/o) outside them, including the nerve roots (radicul/o) that leave the cord. The working cells are neurons, supported by glial cells, named from gli/o, meaning glue.

The brain and cord are wrapped in three membranes, the meninges (mening/o), and cushioned by cerebrospinal fluid. The outermost and toughest membrane is the dura mater, from dur/o, meaning hard. Prefixes place things relative to it: an epidural space lies outside the dura and a subdural space lies beneath it.
Inside the skull, cerebr/o refers to the cerebrum, the large upper part of the brain, and cerebell/o to the cerebellum, which coordinates balance and movement.

Function suffixes describe what the nervous system does. Sensation is esthesi/o, so anesthesia is the absence of sensation. Speech is -phasia, so aphasia is the loss of language ability. Movement problems use -plegia for paralysis and -paresis for partial paralysis or weakness, often with hemi- for one side of the body.
